title: Where the mind is without fear
word: Where the mind is without fear
hookLine: a prayer for a country where the mind is without fear (Gitanjali 35)
tomorrow: what did Tagore's father find blowing past him in the street?

cards: A group chat can go silent the second someone says what everyone's been afraid to say. Tagore once said it to an empire. The British Crown had made him a knight.
Then, at Amritsar, soldiers fired on an unarmed crowd gathered in a walled garden. It's a hard piece of history, so I'll leave the details there.
Tagore wrote to the Viceroy and handed his knighthood back, saying he would rather stand beside his own people.

teach.h: WHAT DOES A FEARLESS MIND NEED?
teach.b: Today's question: what does a mind need to be free of fear?

Tagore answered years before, in Gitanjali's thirty-fifth song: "Where the mind is without fear and the head is held high; Where knowledge is free; Where the world has not been broken up into fragments by narrow domestic walls."

teach.h: MY FATHER, LET MY COUNTRY AWAKE.
teach.b: The song goes on to words that come from the depth of truth and the clear stream of reason, and it ends: "Into that heaven of freedom, my Father, let my country awake." Notice what that makes it. A prayer.
Fearlessness, for Tagore, isn't bravado or a thick skin. It's something asked of God, for a whole people, and it looks like free knowledge, honest words, and walls coming down. Now a neighbor.
Jews and Christians pray Psalm 27, which opens: "The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?" Here is what's shared: both ground fearlessness in God, and both are prayed, not just felt.

And here is the honest difference. The psalmist speaks as one person, surrounded by enemies, asking to dwell in the house of the Lord and be hidden there in trouble. Tagore's prayer names no enemies at all.

It asks for a country's mind to wake up: reason, truth, no narrow walls, a people able to think out loud without looking over their shoulder. One voice speaks from danger, the other for a whole people.

how: Where the mind is without fear is recited in schools and at public gatherings in India and Bangladesh; Psalm 27 is prayed in Jewish and Christian worship, and many Jews add it to daily prayer from the month of Elul through the High Holy Days and Sukkot.

games.q: what does “where the mind is without fear” mean?
o: a soldier's oath to defend his homeland
a prayer for a country with free, fearless minds
a meditation for quieting anxious thoughts

games.q: the prayer and its neighbor: tap the pairs.
p: what Tagore handed back after Amritsar
a prayer for a country without fear
what breaks the world into fragments

s: Where the mind is without fear is a prayer, addressed to 'my Father'
it ends asking God to let the country awake into freedom.
Tagore's song asks only for one person's courage
it prays for a whole country: free knowledge, truth, reason, no narrow walls.
Psalm 27 and Gitanjali 35 say exactly the same thing
both ground fearlessness in God; the psalm asks shelter from enemies, Tagore asks a country's mind to wake.

games.q: a town meeting splits into two camps, and nobody will say what they really think for fear of the other side. what would Tagore's prayer ask for?
o: a room where truth can be spoken without fear, and the walls between camps come down.
that the braver camp wins the vote, so the fear finally ends.
that everyone stays quiet until tempers cool, to keep the peace.
games.why: Gitanjali 35 prays for free knowledge, words from the depth of truth, and a world not broken into fragments by narrow walls.

practice: Name one fear you're carrying into this week, in one plain word. Then raise your right hand, palm open and facing out, the gesture Hindu and Buddhist images call abhaya, do not fear.
Hold it there, easy, not stiff, and let the word sit beside the open hand for two minutes.

wordCard.voice: Where the mind is without fear: Gitanjali's thirty-fifth song, a prayer that a whole country might wake into free knowledge, truth and reason.

orig.note: Sanskrit: fearlessness. The raised open palm in Hindu and Buddhist images, abhaya mudra, means do not fear.

carryVoice: Your line: without fear. Tagore prayed it for a whole country, not only for himself. See you soon.
